title: Opening a Bank Account in Georgia: Cards, Cash, the Lari and the Compliance Desk
excerpt: Bank of Georgia, TBC and Liberty will open a multi-currency GEL/USD/EUR account on a passport and a Georgian phone number, but every foreigner now sits through a compliance questionnaire, and Russian citizens have faced forms, closures and refusals since 2022. Contactless works everywhere down to the metro, the lari swings hard, rent is quoted in dollars, and bills are paid by subscriber number in the app or at a paybox. The trap is the account that gets frozen or closed while you are away.
bodyHtml:
Three banks that matter

Georgian retail banking is a duopoly with a third wheel. Bank of Georgia (orange) and TBC (blue) hold roughly three-quarters of the system between them; Liberty Bank (green) has the widest branch network in the regions and a reputation for being easier on foreigners. All three open multi-currency accounts — one card, separate GEL, USD and EUR balances (Liberty adds GBP), and TBC lets you 'open additional accounts in any other currency of your choice'. Apple Pay has worked here since September 2019 at all three; Google Pay is supported through the TBC and Bank of Georgia apps.

Opening one as a foreigner

On paper it is easy. TBC's expat page says 'you only need a foreign passport and a phone number', and the account 'is opened instantly', with a digital card at once. The phone number must be Georgian — SMS codes will not go to a foreign number — so buy the SIM first. In the branch you will be handed what TBC calls a self-declaration 'on the goal of opening an account and expected banking transactions', and the bank 'may additionally request documents evidencing the source of origin of funds'. This is the compliance questionnaire every foreigner now gets: what do you do, where does the money come from, why Georgia, how much will move through the account each month. Answer consistently and bring a home-bank statement, a lease and proof of income. Since Georgia aligned with FATF rules the National Bank requires each client to be risk-scored, and a decision can take up to two weeks. Citizens of sanctioned countries — Syria, Iran, Afghanistan, North Korea — are refused by default. A residence card with a personal number shortens all of this.

Russian citizens have had a harder time. In April 2022 OC Media reported at least one Bank of Georgia branch requiring Russians to sign a form recognising Russia as 'an aggressor' and 'occupant' of Georgia and Ukraine; from December 2022 all Georgian banks warned clients that accounts used to breach Western sanctions would be blocked without notice, and in April 2023 TBC said it 'reserves the right to close customer accounts without prior notice' if it identifies a sanctions-violating transaction. Refusals for Russian and Belarusian passports are reported but not universal — expect more questions, not an automatic no.

Cards, ATMs and the lari

Contactless is everywhere, down to the Tbilisi metro and buses, which take a tapped bank card directly. ATMs from the big three are dense in the cities and dispense lari; many Bank of Georgia and TBC machines also give dollars from your USD balance. Withdrawing from your own bank is free or nearly so; a foreign card pays a small fee per withdrawal plus whatever your home bank charges.

The lari (GEL, ₾) floats, and it moves. It hit a record low of 3.44 to the dollar in the pandemic, fell to 3.38 in the two weeks after the February 2022 invasion, then rallied to 2.72 by August 2022 on the inflows that came with it. The National Bank publishes an official rate each day at nbg.gov.ge, but it is indicative; the yellow exchange booths on every street set their own and are usually within a whisker of it. The economy is heavily dollarised: landlords quote and often collect rent in USD, and savings sit in dollars. Keep your salary currency in its own balance and convert as you spend rather than in one lump.

Where cash still rules

Bazaars (Dezerter, Navtlugi, Lilo), the neighbourhood fruit stall, most marshrutka minibuses out of town, village guesthouses and the funicular want notes. Keep a couple of hundred lari on you outside the centre.

Getting money in

SWIFT to your USD or EUR balance works from any bank and is how most members are paid. Wise sends to Georgian bank accounts in GEL — 'the recipient gets money in GEL directly from Wise's local bank account' — and the usual remittance systems pay out here. Whether a Georgian resident can hold a full Wise account and card is contested between sources; ⚠ VERIFY on wise.com with your own address. Revolut does not onboard Georgian residents at all as of late 2025, though a Revolut card from home works fine in shops and ATMs.

Paying the rent and the bills

Utilities are tied to a subscriber number (abonenti) on the flat, not to you — ask the landlord for the electricity (Telasi in Tbilisi, Energo-Pro elsewhere), gas (Tbilisi Energy) and water (Georgian Water & Power) numbers on day one. Type them into the Payments section of the bank app and the balance appears; pay in seconds. The same works at the paybox kiosks on every block — blue for TBC, orange for Bank of Georgia, other colours for independents — which take cash for a small commission. Rent goes by bank transfer to the landlord's account or, very commonly, in cash dollars against a signed receipt; a registered lease helps you both.

The quiet-closure trap. A Georgian account is not a set-and-forget thing. Banks re-run their compliance checks — annually, or whenever a transfer looks unusual, and crypto exchanges are a reliable trigger — and send an SMS or email asking for updated documents. The requests are time-limited: miss the window and the account is frozen until you turn up at a branch, sometimes with a fresh source-of-funds file. Accounts that sit idle with no transactions can be closed under the bank's standard terms; ⚠ VERIFY the inactivity period in your own account contract. Keep the Georgian SIM alive — the bank talks to you through it — and log in once a month even when you are away.
